title: Single Responsibility Principle (SRP)
description: Each class/module should own a single responsibility. Mixing concerns (e.g. business logic + persistence + formatting) makes classes fragile and hard to test.
keyPoints: One responsibility → one reason to change.
Split “God classes” by concern (e.g. Order vs OrderRepository vs OrderPrinter).
Improves testability and reuse.
summary: A class should have one, and only one, reason to change.
whenToUse: Whenever a class starts doing “and also…” — extract the extra concern.

title: Open/Closed Principle (OCP)
description: You should be able to add new behavior by adding new code (new subclasses/strategies), not by editing existing, tested code.
keyPoints: Add features via new classes, not by changing old ones.
Achieved with polymorphism/strategies.
Reduces regression risk.
summary: Software entities should be open for extension but closed for modification.
whenToUse: When a switch/if-else grows every time a new type is added — replace with polymorphism.

title: Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP)
description: A subclass should honor the base class’s contract — same expectations, no strengthened preconditions or weakened postconditions. The classic violation: Square extends Rectangle.
keyPoints: Don’t override methods to throw or do nothing.
If a subclass can’t fulfill the contract, the hierarchy is wrong.
Favor composition over a forced “is-a”.
summary: Subtypes must be substitutable for their base types without breaking correctness.
whenToUse: When designing inheritance hierarchies — verify every subclass truly “is-a” base.

title: Interface Segregation Principle (ISP)
description: Prefer many small, focused interfaces over one fat interface, so implementers aren’t forced to stub methods irrelevant to them.
keyPoints: Split fat interfaces by client need.
Avoids “implement-and-throw NotSupported”.
e.g. separate Printer, Scanner, Fax rather than one Machine.
summary: Clients shouldn’t be forced to depend on methods they don’t use.
whenToUse: When implementers keep leaving methods empty/unsupported.

title: Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP)
description: Both high- and low-level modules should depend on interfaces. Inject dependencies rather than constructing them, enabling swapping and testing (mocks).
keyPoints: Program to interfaces; inject implementations.
Enables mocking in tests and swapping providers.
Basis of dependency injection frameworks.
summary: Depend on abstractions, not concretions. High-level modules shouldn’t depend on low-level ones.
whenToUse: Whenever a class “new”s up its collaborators — inject them instead.

title: Singleton
keyPoints: One shared instance (config, connection pool, logger).
Beware: global state hurts testability; make it thread-safe.
summary: Ensure a class has exactly one instance with a global access point.

title: Factory Method
keyPoints: Decouples client from concrete types.
Add new products without changing callers (supports OCP).
summary: Delegate object creation to a method so callers don’t hardcode concrete classes.
whenToUse: When the concrete type to instantiate is decided at runtime by input.

title: Builder
keyPoints: Great for objects with many optional params.
Avoids telescoping constructors; fluent, readable.
summary: Construct a complex object step by step, separating construction from representation.
whenToUse: Objects with many optional fields (e.g. an HTTP request, a Pizza).

title: Strategy
keyPoints: Swap behavior via composition, not if/else chains.
Each strategy is independently testable.
summary: Define a family of interchangeable algorithms and select one at runtime.
whenToUse: Multiple ways to do one thing (payment methods, sort orders, pricing).

title: Observer
keyPoints: One-to-many dependency; publishers don’t know concrete subscribers.
Basis of event systems, pub/sub, MVC.
summary: A subject notifies a list of observers automatically when its state changes.
whenToUse: When many objects must react to another object’s changes (notifications, UI updates).

title: Decorator
keyPoints: Adds behavior without subclass explosion.
Wrappers share the same interface as the wrapped object.
summary: Attach responsibilities to an object dynamically by wrapping it.
whenToUse: Layering optional features (e.g. coffee + milk + sugar; I/O stream wrappers).

title: Adapter
keyPoints: Lets incompatible classes work together.
Wraps a legacy/3rd-party API behind your interface.
summary: Convert one interface into another that clients expect.
whenToUse: Integrating a class whose interface doesn’t match your code.

title: State
keyPoints: Replaces sprawling state-based if/else with state objects.
Each state handles events and decides transitions.
summary: Let an object alter its behavior when its internal state changes — it appears to change class.
whenToUse: Objects with complex state machines (order lifecycle, vending machine, TCP connection).

title: Design a Parking Lot
approach: ParkingLot holds Levels; each Level holds typed ParkingSpots. On entry, find the smallest fitting free spot (polymorphic canFit), mark occupied, create a Ticket with entry time. On exit, FeeCalculator computes the fee from duration; Payment strategy processes it; free the spot. Use Strategy for pricing/payment (OCP) and a Factory for creating Vehicles/Spots. Consider thread-safety on spot allocation (a lock or atomic reservation).
requirements: Assign a vehicle to a fitting free spot; issue a ticket.
Compute fee on exit by duration; support multiple payment types.
summary: The canonical LLD warm-up: model spots, vehicles, tickets, and pricing with clean OO.

title: Design an LRU Cache
approach: Combine a hash map (key → node) for O(1) lookup with a doubly-linked list ordered by recency (MRU at head, LRU at tail). On get/put, move the node to the head; on overflow, remove the tail node and its map entry. The doubly-linked list gives O(1) removal from the middle. (This is also LeetCode 146 — good to know both the interview LLD and the code.)
codeExample: # core: dict + doubly linked list; move-to-front on access, evict tail
requirements: get(key) and put(key, value) both O(1).
Evict least-recently-used entry when at capacity.
Accessing an item makes it most-recently-used.
summary: A fixed-capacity cache evicting the least-recently-used item — O(1) get/put.

title: Design an Elevator System
approach: ElevatorSystem receives requests and a SchedulingStrategy chooses which elevator serves each (nearest in same direction). Each Elevator maintains sorted up/down request sets and sweeps floors (SCAN). Model elevator behavior with the State pattern (Idle/MovingUp/MovingDown/DoorsOpen). Observer can notify displays. Discuss trade-offs of dispatch heuristics.
requirements: Multiple elevators, N floors; internal (car) and external (hall) requests.
Efficiently dispatch and schedule stops (e.g. SCAN/elevator algorithm).
summary: Model elevators, requests, and a dispatcher with a scheduling strategy.

title: Design a Vending Machine
approach: Model the machine as a finite state machine using the State pattern: each State handles events (selectProduct, insertMoney, dispense, cancel) and returns the next state, keeping transition logic out of giant if/else blocks. Inventory tracks stock; a ChangeCalculator returns coins. This cleanly handles edge cases (cancel refunds, out-of-stock).
requirements: Select product, insert money, dispense + return change.
summary: A textbook State-pattern problem: idle → money inserted → dispensing.

title: Design a Rate Limiter (LLD)
approach: Define a RateLimiter interface with allow(clientId); implement algorithms as interchangeable Strategies. TokenBucket stores {tokens, lastRefill} per client, refilling lazily on each call and decrementing if a token is available — guard with a per-client lock or atomic for thread-safety. Discuss where state lives (in-memory vs Redis for distributed) and fail-open vs fail-closed.
summary: The class-level design of a limiter — algorithm behind a clean interface.
